questions.q: Why do ride-sharing systems index driver locations with geohash, quadtree, or H3 cells?
options: The cells encrypt exact positions, protecting driver privacy from riders
Cells turn 2-D proximity search into cheap key lookups of nearby buckets
Cells compress GPS traces efficiently for long-term archival
Cells guarantee equal driver counts in every region
questions.explanation: Mapping lat/lon to a discrete cell id reduces 'who is near me' from an expensive 2-D range scan to reading a handful of hash keys. Cells say nothing about density, so counts per cell vary widely.

questions.q: How often do driver apps typically report location, and how?
options: Once per trip, bundled with the final receipt upload
Continuously, via HTTP long-polling connections initiated by the server
Every few seconds via lightweight pings over a persistent connection
Only when the driver manually refreshes the app
questions.explanation: Matching and live tracking need near-current positions, so drivers emit small pings every few seconds over a long-lived socket, avoiding per-request connection setup cost.

questions.q: Where does the freshest driver-location state usually live?
options: In the relational trips table, updated on every location ping
In each rider's app, synced peer-to-peer
In a data warehouse fed by hourly batches
In an in-memory store keyed by geo cell, with short TTLs
questions.explanation: Locations are high-write, short-lived, and read by proximity, which suits an in-memory geo index with TTL eviction. Writing every ping to a relational table would overwhelm it.

questions.q: What is the basic matching flow after a rider requests a pickup?
options: Query nearby cells for candidate drivers, rank them, offer the job
Broadcast the pickup request to every online driver in the city at once
Assign the driver who has been idle longest anywhere
Queue the request until a driver searches for riders
questions.explanation: Matching narrows to a local candidate set from nearby cells, ranks by ETA, rating, and acceptance likelihood, then dispatches offers. Citywide broadcast wastes bandwidth and produces poor matches.

questions.q: Why is straight-line (haversine) distance a poor ETA basis?
options: GPS coordinates drift too much for reliable distance math
It ignores the earth's curvature over city scales
It cannot be computed quickly at matching volume
Roads, one-ways, and traffic make travel distance and time differ from it
questions.explanation: Vehicles follow a road network, so rivers, one-way streets, and congestion can make a driver 500m away a ten-minute drive. Haversine is fast and curvature-aware; it just is not the travel path.

questions.q: What is surge pricing's primary system purpose?
options: Balance supply and demand by pricing when riders outnumber drivers
Recover the platform's infrastructure costs during recurring traffic peaks
Reward loyal riders with predictable peak pricing
Throttle API traffic during major city events
questions.explanation: A higher multiplier simultaneously damps marginal demand and pulls drivers toward the undersupplied zone, clearing the local market rather than leaving riders queued indefinitely.

questions.q: Rider apps show the driver's car moving smoothly toward pickup. What powers this?
options: The rider's app extrapolates positions from the trip's original route plan
A peer-to-peer link established between the two phones
Server-pushed location updates over a socket, interpolated client-side
Frequent full-page refreshes against a REST endpoint
questions.explanation: The server pushes discrete pings every few seconds and the client animates between them along the road geometry, so sparse real data reads as continuous motion.

questions.q: Which pair of state machines sits at the heart of the trip domain?
options: Payment ledger states and invoice states
Driver states (offline/available/on-trip) and trip states (requested to completed)
Map tile states and route cache states
Session states for the rider app and push-token states
questions.explanation: Driver availability and trip lifecycle are the two coupled state machines that govern dispatch: transitions must be legal and atomic so a driver is never on two trips at once.

questions.q: A downtown cell floods with drivers; neighbor cells are empty. Fixed search over one cell misses matches. What's the standard fix?
options: Expand the search ring over neighboring cells until enough candidates found
Shrink the global cell size so that the dense cell splits automatically
Cache the last successful match radius per rider
Reassign idle drivers' cells randomly every minute
questions.explanation: Querying successively wider rings of neighbor cells until the candidate pool is large enough adapts naturally to any density. Changing the global cell size just moves the imbalance elsewhere.

questions.q: Location pings arrive at 1M/sec citywide. Which ingestion design fits?
options: Direct synchronous writes into a relational database per ping
Batching pings hourly into object storage before matching
One WebSocket server instance holding all driver state
A partitioned stream/queue feeding in-memory geo indexes
questions.explanation: A partitioned log absorbs the write burst, scales horizontally by key, and decouples producers from the geo index consumers. Hourly batching destroys the freshness matching depends on.

questions.q: Two matchers concurrently offer the same driver to two riders. What prevents a double booking?
options: Riders confirm manually, resolving conflicts by phone
An atomic claim (lock or compare-and-set) on the driver's state before dispatch
Randomized offer delays that make collisions unlikely
Eventually consistent replication that later merges both trip records into one
questions.explanation: Only one matcher may flip the driver from available to reserved, so a compare-and-set or lease on that record makes the loser back off and pick another driver. Random delays reduce but never eliminate races.

questions.q: Choosing between geohash and H3 for supply indexing, what is H3's noted advantage?
options: H3 cell identifiers are strings, so they sort lexicographically by proximity
H3 is lossless while geohash truncates coordinates
Hexagonal cells have more uniform neighbor distances than rectangles
H3 requires no library support in mobile clients
questions.explanation: A hexagon has six neighbors all at equal center distance, whereas a square's diagonal neighbors are farther than its edge neighbors, making ring expansion a cleaner approximation of a circle.

questions.q: ETA service must respond in ~50ms during matching. Full shortest-path routing is too slow. What's the standard approach?
options: Run Dijkstra on the raw road graph for every request
Ask drivers to self-report their expected arrival times
Precomputed hierarchical routing (contraction hierarchies) plus live traffic adjustments
Straight-line distance divided by the city's average speed
questions.explanation: Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcut edges offline so a query touches a tiny fraction of the graph, and live traffic speeds are layered on the resulting path for an accurate time.

questions.q: Surge computation needs demand per zone in near real time. Which pipeline fits?
options: Nightly batch jobs recomputing zone multipliers
Windowed stream aggregation of requests and supply per cell
Synchronous counting inside the matching transaction
Sampling one percent of ride requests and extrapolating on a weekly basis
questions.explanation: Tumbling or sliding windows over the request and driver-status streams give per-cell supply/demand ratios updated every few minutes, which is exactly the cadence surge needs.

questions.q: A driver's phone loses connectivity mid-trip for 3 minutes. What should the system do?
options: Cancel the trip and refund the rider automatically
Immediately reassign the trip to the nearest available driver
Mark the driver banned pending a support review
Keep trip state server-side, tolerate the gap, reconcile pings on reconnect
questions.explanation: Connectivity gaps are routine in tunnels and garages, and the ride is physically still happening, so the server holds trip state and the app replays buffered pings on reconnect.

questions.q: Matching optimizes for nearest driver, but city-wide efficiency sometimes prefers a slightly farther driver. Why?
options: Global assignment can cut total wait: greedy local picks strand later riders
Farther drivers accept offers at higher rates in all markets
Nearest-driver assignment logic violates fairness regulations in most large cities
GPS error makes the nearest driver impossible to determine
questions.explanation: Batching requests and solving a global assignment minimizes total wait, since a greedy grab can consume the only driver who was uniquely close to another rider.

questions.q: Capacity: 300k concurrent drivers ping every 4 seconds. What ingest rate must location intake sustain?
options: About 1,200 pings per second
About 7,500 pings per second
About 300,000 pings per second
About 75,000 pings per second
questions.explanation: Each driver contributes 1/4 ping per second, so 300,000 divided by 4 gives 75,000 pings per second sustained.

questions.q: The geo index node for the airport cell keeps hot-spotting during holiday peaks. Which mitigation preserves query correctness?
options: Split the hot cell to a finer resolution and spread sub-cells across nodes
Drop every other ping from airport drivers at ingestion
Route airport queries to a read replica lagging by a minute
Serve matching during peaks from a cached copy of yesterday's airport driver list
questions.explanation: Subdividing the hot cell and distributing the children spreads load without losing any driver data, unlike dropping pings or serving stale lists, which produce wrong matches.

questions.q: Trip events (request, accept, pickup, dropoff) feed billing, analytics, and safety, which need them reliably and in order per trip. Which backbone fits?
options: Fire-and-forget UDP multicast to all consumer groups
Direct synchronous REST calls from the trip service to every consumer
A partitioned event log keyed by trip ID with consumer offsets
A shared table each consumer polls and deletes rows from
questions.explanation: Keying by trip ID puts one trip's events in a single partition, which guarantees per-trip ordering, while durable per-consumer offsets let billing and analytics replay independently.

questions.q: During a citywide outage of the matching service, which degradation preserves the most business value?
options: Reject all new ride requests instantly so riders switch to competitors' apps
Queue requests with honest wait estimates and match when capacity returns
Silently accept requests and match them in random order later
Fail over matching into the rider mobile apps via peer discovery
questions.explanation: Holding demand with a transparent wait keeps riders on the platform and lets matching drain the backlog on recovery. Silent acceptance without honest estimates just converts the outage into broken promises.
